signal.title: [doc][kuberay] Migrate ray.io/v1alpha1 examples to ray.io/v1
signal.text: ## Why this change is needed Ray's user-facing KubeRay examples still ship `apiVersion: ray.io/v1alpha1`, including the canonical RayCluster configuration guide. `ray.io/v1alpha1` is served but is not the storage version, has been feature-frozen since December 2023, and exposes far fewer fields than `ray.io/v1`. Readers who copy these examples land on the frozen version and silently lose access to everything added since, including `authOptions`, `tlsOptions`, `networkPolicy`, `gcsFaultToleranceOptions`, `historyServerOptions`, and the upgrade strategies. ## What changed **Docs examples** — `config.md`, four snippets in the Serve fault-tolerance guide, and the two `doc_code` manifests move to `ray.io/v1`. `RayClusterSpec` in v1 is a strict superset of v1alpha1, so the RayCluster examples needed no field changes. **A latent bug in `k8s_config.yaml`** — the manifest used `serveConfig`, which is absent from the CRD schema in *both* `ray.io/v1` and `ray.io/v1alpha1`. Kubernetes prunes it on a structural schema, so the documented example deploys a RayService with zero applications. Converted to `serveConfigV2`. Also dropped `serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold` and `deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold`, which KubeRay's types mark as no longer used. **`KUBERAY_CRD_VER` default** — flipped from `v1alpha1` to `v1`. KubeRay has injected `KUBERAY_CRD_VER=v1` into the autoscaler sidecar since kuberay#1496 (October 2023), so this default only applies when an operator predating that release omits the variable. **Image pins in `config.md` (added after first review request)** — the condensed RayCluster reference also pinned `rayVersion: "2.3.0"` and `rayproject/ray-ml:2.3.0`. `rayproject/ray-ml` is no longer published publicly: versioned tags stop at `2.30.0` (`2.31.0` onward all 404) and Ray pushed 16 `2.46.0.deprecated*` markers on 2025-05-07. Since this PR was already rewriting that example, both moved to `rayproject/ray:2.56.1` with `rayVersion` kept in sync, which is what the page's own prose requires. Verified `rayproject/ray:2.56.1` resolves on Docker Hub. Floating and stale pins in other doc files are handled separately in #65339. **Recorded output left alone** — the pasted controller log in `rayservice-troubleshooting.md` and the commented `kubectl get podgroup` output in `volcano.md` are historical captures of operator output, not input a reader applies. Editing them would falsify a quote. **Release test template (last commit)** — migrated for consistency, but this is cosmetic: `k8s_serve_ha_test` is `frequency: manual` and has been failing since October 2024 (#36190), and its `solution.py` imports `ray.serve.drivers.DAGDriver`, which no longer exists. Details in https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/36190#issuecomment-5244475555. Happy to drop this commit if Serve would rather handle the whole test separately. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "v1alpha1"` returns nothing. The related KubeRay-side issue (ray-project/kuberay#5091) covers generated API-reference cross-links, not these examples. #36190 is the existing tracking issue for the release test; I commented there rather than opening a competing issue. ## Testing ``` pytest python/ray/tests/kuberay/ -q # 76 passed ``` The only failure in that directory is `test_autoscaling_e2e.py`, which requires a live Kubernetes cluster and a `rayci/` runner path; it reads a fixture this PR does not touch. Additional verification: - All four changed manifests validate against KubeRay's real `ray.io/v1` CRD schemas (`ray-operator/config/crd/bases/`). - All three `serveConfigV2` blocks validate against `ray.serve.schema.ServeDeploySchema`. - The release-test template still renders through `str.format` and parses afterward. - Confirmed directly that `serveConfig` is absent from the v1 `RayService` spec schema and `serveConfigV2` is present. ## AI assistance AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to research the v1/v1alpha1 delta against the KubeRay source, locate the affected files, and draft these changes. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.
signal.author: dstrodtman

signal.title: [docs] Add Kubernetes and KubeRay conventions to the style guide
signal.text: ## Why this change Ray on Kubernetes docs describe Kubernetes API objects alongside Ray concepts, and the two vocabularies collide. Deployment, Job, and Service each name both a Kubernetes API object and a distinct Ray concept, so capitalization is the only thing telling them apart, and the style guide didn't say which form to use where. A contributor asking "RayCluster or Ray cluster?" had to derive the answer from two guides and adjudicate between them. This adds a `Writing Ray on Kubernetes and KubeRay docs` section to the style guide, scoped to the user-facing pages under `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/` and the contributor-facing pages in [ray-project/kuberay](https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay). The approach is to extend this guide with a Kubernetes deference section rather than stand up a separate KubeRay style guide. The two guides already overlap heavily, and a forked guide would drift within a release or two. ## What the casing scan found The term list isn't invented. It comes from a prose-only scan of three corpora: 79 user-facing pages in this repo, 12 contributor pages in `ray-project/kuberay`, and 128 pages of `kubernetes/website` (`content/en/docs/concepts/`, commit `bb38117c0`). The scan strips front matter, fenced code blocks, inline code, MyST roles, and link targets before counting, so YAML field names and CLI output don't inflate the figures. Headline: **these docs already follow the Kubernetes casing rule.** Upstream Kubernetes capitalizes "Pod" in 71% of prose uses; the Ray-side KubeRay docs do so in 70%. So this PR documents a rule the docs mostly already follow, and does not propose a capitalization sweep. | Term | Ray-side KubeRay docs | Upstream Kubernetes | Read | |---|---|---|---| | Pod | 371/527 (70%) | 3712/5195 (71%) | Matches upstream almost exactly. | | ConfigMap | 20/21 (95%) | 119/130 (91%) | Healthy. | | Ingress | 8/15 (53%) | 148/242 (61%) | Roughly aligned. | | Service | 18/114 (15%) | 515/946 (54%) | Diverges by design. | | Job | 17/143 (11%) | 522/610 (85%) | Diverges by design. | | Deployment | 6/53 (11%) | 355/461 (77%) | Diverges by design. | The three "diverges by design" rows are the reason this section exists. Sampling shows the lowercase uses are Ray Serve deployments, Ray jobs, and Ray services, not Kubernetes API objects. That's a naming collision, not drift, so the fix is a disambiguation rule rather than a sweep. Kubernetes's own rule expects a mix (UpperCamelCase for the API object, sentence case for the general concept), which is why the upstream column isn't 100% either. The one genuine inconsistency the scan found is **"Ray Autoscaler" (44 uses) against "Ray autoscaler" (35)**, spread across at least eight files. This guide already says to lowercase generic nouns even when they name a Ray concept, so lowercase wins. Recording the rule here is the prerequisite for a mechanical follow-up cleanup. I've left that out of this PR to keep the rule change reviewable on its own. ## Open questions for reviewers I've deliberately written only the rules I can support from the two published guides plus the scan. These five are genuinely open, and I'd rather resolve them in review than assert them: All five are now resolved in review. Each entry keeps the original question for context, since the reasoning behind the answer matters more than the answer: 1. ~~**Confirm the custom-resource split.**~~ **Resolved** by @win5923: the split is intentional and consistent with Kubernetes terminology. Original question: The section documents `RayCluster` (the resource) versus "Ray cluster" (the running thing it produces), currently 335 against 106 uses in this repo. I read it as intentional and matching the Kubernetes API-object rule. Worth confirming rather than normalizing to one form. 1. ~~**"head Pod" versus "head node."**~~ **Resolved** by @win5923: use "head Pod" consistently when a Ray cluster runs on Kubernetes. Original question: The section prefers "head Pod" for the Kubernetes-hosted case, since a node is a machine on Kubernetes. `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/index.md` currently says "a head node pod and a collection of worker node pods," which stacks both vocabularies. Reasonable, or is "head node" worth keeping for continuity with Ray's core architecture docs? 1. ~~**Feature graduation phases.**~~ **Resolved** by @win5923: keep the existing convention, start case for Kubernetes feature stages and lowercase for Ray and KubeRay stages. The corpus already works this way. I've added the ownership test for the ambiguous case, a third-party controller's feature gate, which makes `kueue.md:747` a defect rather than an exception. No Vale rule, since a substitution can't tell which project a stage name refers to. Original question: Kubernetes uses start case ("DRA is Beta"); Ray docs lowercase feature stages. This bites on pages discussing a Kubernetes feature's stage and a Ray feature's stage in one paragraph. I left it out of the section rather than pick. Which wins? 1. ~~**Field values.**~~ **Resolved** by @win5923, who writes values in backticks: "set `upgradeStrategy.type` to `NewClusterWithIncrementalUpgrade`." That's also what this guide already says, so the section now states the divergence from Kubernetes explicitly rather than leaving the two guides to contradict each other silently. Original question: Kubernetes wants unquoted, unstyled values ("set `imagePullPolicy` to Always"); this guide says to use backticks for configuration values and gives `num_replicas: 1`. These are closer than they look, since one is a bare value and the other a key-value pair, but the guidance should say which form applies where. 1. ~~**"Ray dashboard" versus "Ray Dashboard"**~~ **Resolved** by @win5923: lowercase, on the grounds that "dashboard" is a generic noun for the same reason "autoscaler" is, which makes the rule already in this guide cover it. Applies to "KubeRay dashboard" too. This is the largest defect the ruleset now surfaces, at 43 prose uses plus 1, and it moves `KubeRay.Terms` on these pages from 160 to 204. A fair number sit in headings, where the sentence-case rule makes them defects too. Sweep folds into #65423. Original question: 43 title-case against 18 lowercase. This guide implies lowercase, but the dashboard is arguably a named UI surface. Not addressed in the section pending a call. Two further items are out of scope here but worth flagging: - **Line wrapping in the `kuberay` repo.** This guide requires soft wrap. The Kubernetes guide requires manual wrap, justified by localization teams diffing per line, which KubeRay doesn't have. Nothing in this PR changes that, since this guide already governs `doc/source/`. But `kuberay`'s `.markdownlint.yaml` sets `MD013` to 120 characters via pre-commit, which is a latent gate: 266 lines in its `docs/` already exceed it, it isn't enforced in CI, and it isn't auto-fixable, so contributors hit it unpredictably on whichever file they touch. Disabling it there would align the two repos, but that's a call for KubeRay maintainers in their own repo. - **Turning Vale enforcement on.** This PR now adds the ruleset but doesn't enforce it. See the section below. ## Staged Vale ruleset A later commit adds a Vale ruleset for these pages, following the pattern already used for the Ray Data docs. **Nothing is enforced yet.** The Vale hook in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` stays scoped to `^doc/source/data/.*`, so CI checks exactly what it checked before. - `.vale/styles/config/vocabularies/KubeRay/accept.txt` — the KubeRay custom resources, the Kubernetes and ecosystem API objects these pages reference, and project names. Skips what the `General` vocabulary already accepts (`Kubernetes`, `kubectl`, `CRD(s)?`, `namespace`). - `.vale/styles/KubeRay/Terms.yml` — a `substitution` rule at `warning` level covering only the casing forms the new style-guide section settles, with `vocab: false` (see below). The open questions above are deliberately absent. - `.vale.ini` — registers the vocabulary and scopes the style to `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/`. Registering a vocabulary that the hook doesn't exercise matches existing practice here: `RLlib` and `Train` are already in `Vocab` while the hook only runs on `doc/source/data/`. Contributors can run it by hand today: ``` vale doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/ ``` To enforce later, widen the `files` pattern on the `vale` hook. I'd still hold that until the open questions land. ### What I verified Vale 3.12.0 locally. **Path scoping works.** The KubeRay rules fire on a file under `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/` and stay silent on identical content at the repo root. **Current state of these pages** — 146 `KubeRay.Terms` alerts, which lines up with the casing scan: | Alert | Count | |---|---| | Use 'Ray autoscaler' instead of 'Ray Autoscaler' | 42 | | Use 'head Pod' instead of 'head pod' | 20 | | Use 'worker Pod' instead of 'worker pod' | 7 | | Use 'Ray job' instead of 'ray job' | 2 | | Use 'Ray Serve' instead of 'Ray serve' | 1 | | Use 'Ray cluster' instead of 'ray cluster' | 1 | | Use 'KubeRay' instead of 'Kuberay' | 1 | | Use 'GCS fault tolerance' instead of 'GCS FT' | 1 | The 42 matches the scan's count for these pages exactly, which is a useful cross-check on both. None of it is enforced, so nothing here has to be fixed in this PR. **No regression on the gated path.** Alert count on `doc/source/data/` goes 174 → 173, deterministic across repeated runs in both states, with no new alerts. A `Vocab` list is global, so it can only widen what's accepted. The single alert that disappears is a `Google.Parens` hit in `concurrent-dataset-execution.md`; no term in the new vocabulary appears on that line, so I'm reporting that as observed rather than claiming I understand the mechanism. It's a reduction either way, so it can't break the gate. ### The vocabulary shadowing trap Worth knowing if you write Vale rules here: a `Vocab` accept entry shadows its token for **every** rule, case-insensitively. A substitution whose target appears in an accept list silently never fires, and nothing warns you. This bit the `Ray Autoscaler` swap, because `autoscaler` is accepted in `config/vocabularies/Data/accept.txt`. The fix is `vocab: false` on the rule, which opts out of the filtering without touching the Data vocabulary. The rule carries a comment saying so. Credit to Bugbot for catching it. I'd first shipped that swap commented out, having concluded the only way to enable it was dropping `autoscaler` from the Data vocabulary and accepting new spelling alerts on the gated path. That was wrong, and `vocab: false` avoids the tradeoff entirely. ## Added after review Two rules that review surfaced, both in the style-guide section plus the Vale ruleset. **Node stays lowercase.** Node is a Kubernetes API object, so "capitalize Kubernetes API objects" read literally tells contributors to write "Kubernetes Node." These pages almost always mean the machine, and all 24 uses are correctly lowercase today, so a literal reading of the rule would have someone "fix" working prose into wrongness. Kubernetes applies the same two-part rule it applies elsewhere, capitalizing Node only for the resource, and the section now says so. **Don't write "Ray Pod."** This answers the casing question raised in review, and the answer turned out to be neither casing. A Pod is a Kubernetes host that contains a Ray node plus any sidecars, so naming it after Ray overstates what it is. "TPU Pod" also already occupies the qualified-Pod form in these pages and means a group of TPU chips rather than a Kubernetes object. The term had no settled form to preserve either: across the 55 prose lines using it, casing split four ways at 20, 16, 16, and 15. Stating that alone would be a trap, because a bare "Pod" isn't always an adequate replacement, so the section gives the test that separates the cases: - Qualify when the qualifier distinguishes two referents. That's why "Ray node" against "Kubernetes node" is correct and should stay. - Don't qualify when it relabels one thing. - Keep the scope explicit where a page also describes Pods the RayCluster doesn't own, such as the operator, Redis, or a `curl` Pod, and where a nearby command filters by label. "List all Pods" and "List the Ray cluster's Pods" describe different commands and shouldn't read the same way. The cleanup is #65423, which removes all 89 uses from the docs and is reviewable on its own. This PR is the rule; that one is the sweep. Vale picks up four swaps for the retired forms. Plurals get their own entries, for the word-boundary reason @win5923 identified on the `head pod` swaps. Verified that they don't fire on "Ray head Pod" or "Ray worker Pods", and that the gated `doc/source/data/` path holds at 173 alerts. ## Not a duplicate Checked open PRs for this area before starting: ``` gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "writing-style" gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "style guide in:title" gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "kuberay style" ``` No open PR touches `doc/source/ray-contribute/writing-style.md` or proposes KubeRay style guidance. The `writing-style` matches were all false positives on `write_delta`. This extends the guide added in #64518. ## Testing ``` pre-commit run --files doc/source/ray-contribute/writing-style.md ``` Passes, but as a no-op on the Markdown: every hook reports "no files to check," because no pre-commit hook applies to Markdown under `doc/source/` and Vale is scoped to `doc/source/data/`. Stating that plainly instead of claiming coverage it doesn't give. The Vale config files do have hook coverage, and those checks ran for real: ``` pre-commit run --files .vale.ini .vale/styles/KubeRay/Terms.yml .vale/styles/config/vocabularies/KubeRay/accept.txt ``` `trim trailing whitespace`, `fix end of files`, `check for added large files`, and `semgrep` all pass. Vale verification for the ruleset is in the section above: path scoping, the 31-alert current state, and the 174 → 173 no-regression check on the gated path. Verified by hand: the new `(kubernetes-docs-style)=` anchor doesn't collide with any existing target in `doc/source/`, and the section uses the same MyST anchor form and Markdown pipe-table style already used elsewhere in this file. Rendering is verified by the Read the Docs preview build on this PR. No code, no API, no behavior change. The prose is a contributor guide; the Vale files add configuration without widening what CI enforces. ## AI assistance Written with AI assistance (Claude). I've reviewed every changed line, generated and inspected the casing counts myself, and can defend the change end to end. The scan scripts that produced the numbers live outside this repo; happy to share the methodology or re-run against a different corpus if a reviewer wants to check a figure. --- ### Update: the vocabulary now covers the ecosystem terms these pages use (555ebdad) Running `vale doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/`, which this PR's `.vale.ini` comment tells contributors to do, produced 215 `Vale.Spelling` alerts on correctly spelled terms. The accept list covered API objects, the custom resources, and project names, but not the wider ecosystem vocabulary the pages actually contain. Left as is, a contributor following the instruction learns to ignore Vale on exactly the paths this PR wants gated. Added: the ecosystem projects (Istio, Kiali, gVisor, Kata, Krew, Kustomize, Bottlerocket, Aliyun, GCSFuse, Promtail, Fluentd, Filebeat, Alertmanager), the Gateway API `HTTPRoute`, and the Kubernetes and infrastructure terms in use (cgroup, finalizer, kubeconfig, kubelet, namespaced, namespaces, toleration, upscaling, downscaling, vCPU, FQDN, AMI, subnet, syscall, hostname, cron, CA, autoscalers). **Excluded on purpose, since an accept list shouldn't launder a defect.** `CR` and `CRs`, 12 uses, because this PR's own guidance says to write "custom resource" and to define CustomResourceDefinition then use CRD. Real misspellings: `heterogenous`, `replicaset` for ReplicaSet, `Deepseek` for DeepSeek, `nodepool` for node pool. `gsutil`, which `gcloud storage` supersedes. Unbackticked code identifiers, which are a formatting defect rather than a vocabulary gap: `podSpec`, `podSelector`, `nodeSelector`, `jsonPointers`, `intervalSeconds`, `workerGroup`, `ignoreDifferences`, `HTTPMode`, `args`, `yaml`. And generic English that Vale's dictionary lacks, which belongs in the General vocabulary rather than a KubeRay-specific one. Three entries are case-tolerant (`[Tt]oleration(s)?`, `[Uu]pscaling`, `[Dd]ownscaling`). A lowercase-only entry makes `Vale.Terms` flag the legitimate sentence-start capitalization. **Verification**, deterministic across repeated runs: - `doc/source/cluster/kubernetes/`: 1329 alerts to 1178. `Vale.Spelling` drops from 215 to 72. `KubeRay.Terms` is unchanged at 160, confirming no swap got shadowed by a new accept entry, which is the trap the `Ray Autoscaler` comment in `Terms.yml` documents. - `doc/source/data/`, the only path the pre-commit hook gates: 173 to 170, with **no new alerts**. A `Vocab` is global, so it can only widen what's accepted. - One candidate entry was dropped for exactly that reason. A `runtime(s)?` entry made `Vale.Terms` flag "Runtime" in `doc/source/data/monitoring-your-workload.rst`, a new alert on the gated path. Four new `Vale.Terms` alerts do appear on the KubeRay paths, and all four are genuine casing defects in existing pages rather than noise: "Kubelet" twice in `configuring-ippr.md`, lowercase "istio" naming the project in `rayservice-incremental-upgrade.md`, and "Cgroups" in the `resource-isolation-with-writable-cgroups.md` H1, which is also title case. Those are content fixes for a separate change, not this one. AI assistance was used for this commit, including the Vale sweep and the before-and-after verification above.

signal.title: [train] Share PlacementGroupCleaner across Train runs
signal.text: ## Description Ray Train v2 currently creates one detached `PlacementGroupCleaner` actor per Train controller. Since cleaners are pinned to the head node, their memory use grows linearly with concurrent Train runs. In the workload described in #65443, 24 cleaners use approximately 14.4 GB on the head node. This PR replaces the per-controller actors with one cluster-wide shared cleaner. The cleaner tracks controllers independently, so a failed controller only triggers cleanup for its own placement groups. The shared cleaner: - uses a fixed, versioned name and internal namespace with `get_if_exists=True`; - remains detached, pinned to the head node, and scheduled outside captured placement groups; - persists controller and placement-group registrations in GCS internal KV; - restores active and incomplete cleanup records after actor restart; - rejects late placement-group registration after controller death; - isolates State API and placement-group cleanup failures between controllers; - scopes State API queries to its own cluster when multiple clusters are active. ## Related issues Fixes #65443. ## Testing ```text PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # 16 passed PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_controller_callback_behaviour.py # 10 passed pre-commit run --files \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/callbacks/placement_group_callback.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/execution/controller/placement_group_cleaner.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/state/util.py \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # Passed git diff --check origin/master...HEAD # Passed ``` A local end-to-end multi-job scenario used two independent drivers, each running a real Train v2 `DataParallelTrainer` with a controller, worker, and placement group. Both runs shared one cleaner. After one driver was killed, only its placement group was removed; the other run remained active and completed normally. The cleaner stayed alive throughout. ## Contribution notes No other open PR referencing #65443 or matching this PlacementGroupCleaner change was found before requesting review. AI assistance was used for implementation, testing, and self-review of this change.

signal.title: [core] Free local objects batching
signal.text: ## Description When object refcount goes to zero or internal free, FreeObjectOnNodesAsync will be triggered to send RPCs to where data actually lives to free up space. This PR batch FreeObject RPC to reduce driver's work. ## Additional Information ### Semantics change in the happy path, where no network parition, no raylet failure, the semantics is the same. Under different failures, the behavior might be different. 1. The RPC connection is broken because of temporal network partition: retryable rpc will keep retry past rpc while new free object rpc will be queued in free_in_flight_. Eventually, if the node is determined as dead by GCS, it goes to case 2, otherwise it will keep retrying. 2. The node is determined as dead by GCS, then all the free rpc queued in free_in_flight_ to the dead node will be dropped, this is the same as previous behavior. More specifically there are two paths, the first is in SendFreeLocalObjectsBatchIfNeeded, if the node is dead determined by GCS, `GetRayletRpcClient(node)` will return null and `free_in_flight_` and `free_pending_` of that node are both cleared. Second, if a node dies when an free RPC is in-flight, `raylet_client_pool->Disconnect(node)` got triggered, `client_map_` drops the ref of raylet client. When RayletClient goes to 0, for `RetryableGrpcClient`, all the pending RPC in `RetryableGrpcClient` will receive `Status::Disconnected`, thus trigger the callback of `FreeLocalObjects` implemented in this PR to drain `free_in_flight_` and `free_pending_` queue of the dead node. 3. Coreworker (i.e., the owner itself) is down: a separate path (NodeManager::NodeRemoved or NodeManager::HandleUnexpectedWorkerFailure, depends on owner worker or the node failure) in raylet will do the cleanup. GCS will publish the node/worker death info to other nodes in the cluster so that they can do local cleanup of objects. ### Design Space To batch free RPC requests, we have two axis: 1. batching timing, we can do - batching by a time window, OR - batching all requests when there are requests still in flight. 2. batching granularity: - By (oid + number of copies): track the total number of (object, copy) frees pending across all nodes, and flush based on that global count. - Per-node: keep one queue and at most one in-flight FreeLocalObjects RPC per node; a batch is the set of object ids to free on that specific node. For batching timing, using time window will introduce a magic number, so we didn't choose that. For batching granularity we do per-node, since global-count batching keeps sending to unreachable nodes regardless of network state, so the backlog accumulates inside the retryable-RPC layer (hard to observe); per-node keeps one in-flight per node and leaves the rest in our own inspectable free_pending_ queue. ### Performance test I write a [script](https://github.com/ShockYoungCHN/ray/blob/free-local-objects-benchmark/free_local_objects_driver_benchmark.py) at that release 1 mil objects and profile the driver usage at the same time. At the above flamegraph, `CoreWorker::FreeObjectOnNodesAsync` takes 59% share of driver samples, at the below one, it's negligible. The number of rpc calls also go down ~255 times, which is pretty much the same as how large each free obj batch is (i.e., 256).

signal.title: [Data] Fused map functions are serialized with every shuffle-map task
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen When Ray Data fuses a `MapOperator` into `RandomShuffle` or shuffle-based `Repartition`, the fused upstream map function is stored directly in `ShuffleTaskSpec.map_args`. Pull- and push-based schedulers expand those args into every shuffle-map task submission. A UDF that captures large immutable state is therefore serialized once per shuffle-map task. Currently, a 100 MiB captured closure with 10 input blocks reached about 1004 MiB incremental peak object-store usage in a local pull-shuffle benchmark. The fix reduced the same case to about 104 MiB. The growth is approximately closure size multiplied by map-task count. It should serialize the fused map function once, store it in Ray's object store, and pass its `ObjectRef` as a top-level positional argument to each shuffle-map task. Ray Core should resolve the function before invoking the task. ### Versions / Dependencies on `master` ### Reproduction script ```python import numpy as np import ray state = np.ones(100 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=np.uint8) def udf(batch): assert state[0] == 1 return batch ray.init(num_cpus=4) ( ray.data.range(500_000, override_num_blocks=10) .map_batches(udf, batch_size=None, batch_format="numpy") .random_shuffle(seed=0) .materialize() ) ``` ### Issue Severity Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

signal.title: [Data] Throttle OutputBackpressureGuard releases with a per-op interval
signal.text: ## Description **Summary:** Add an opt-in, per-operator minimum interval between `OutputBackpressureGuard` releases so the liveness escape hatch can't defeat backpressure on large-block workloads. Disabled by default; no behavior change unless configured. `OutputBackpressureGuard` is a liveness escape hatch: when backpressure policies clamp an operator's output budget to 0 bytes, the guard flips it to 1 byte so the executor emits one more block and the pipeline can't deadlock. This check runs on every scheduling iteration, so whenever the guard keeps voting to release, an operator effectively emits a block per iteration. On workloads with very large blocks (e.g. rows carrying raw audio buffers), that per-iteration release rate can outpace how fast downstream drains. At that point the escape hatch effectively defeats the backpressure it's meant to be a narrow exception to: the policies say "0 bytes", but the operator keeps emitting a large block every iteration anyway. Object store usage then grows unbounded even though the pipeline is nominally under backpressure, pushing the store toward spilling / OOM. This PR adds an opt-in, per-operator **minimum interval between successive guard releases**. With a positive interval, the guard releases an operator at most once per interval, giving downstream time to drain between unblocks. The first release for each operator is never throttled, and idle-detection remains the liveness fallback, so pipeline liveness is preserved. The feature is disabled by default (`None`), so existing behavior is unchanged. ## Related issues <!-- Link an issue if one is filed, e.g. "Related to #XXXXX". --> ## Additional information **New configuration** - `DataContext.output_backpressure_guard_release_interval_s: Optional[float]` - Env var: `RAY_DATA_OUTPUT_BACKPRESSURE_GUARD_RELEASE_INTERVAL_S` - Default: `None` (no throttling — legacy behavior). Non-positive values also disable it. **Usage** ```python import ray ctx = ray.data.DataContext.get_current() # Release a fully-throttled operator at most once every 300s. ctx.output_backpressure_guard_release_interval_s = 300 ```

signal.title: [data] Fanout into independently schedulable one-row blocks has very high overhead
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen We have Ray Data pipelines where each row represents a user-defined unit of work, such as one file-processing or model-inference task. For these pipelines, **one row per physical block is a scheduling contract, not a block-size tuning preference**. Ray Data schedules map tasks and actor calls from physical input blocks. If a block contains 10,000 rows, then `map_batches(batch_size=1)` can invoke the UDF on one row at a time, but those invocations are performed serially inside the Ray worker processing that block. They are not 10,000 independently schedulable Ray tasks or actor calls. After fanout, we therefore need: ``` N physical blocks, one row each -> each input row produces Mi Task rows -> sum(Mi) physical blocks, one row each -> downstream CPU or GPU workers can process every Task independently ``` `Mi` may be zero. Users choose the Task granularity; they should not need to choose an internal Ray chunk size. I expected Ray Data to deliver these independently schedulable outputs fast enough to keep an ordinary downstream task or autoscaling actor pool busy. Instead, producing and consuming many one-row blocks has very high end-to-end overhead. This is especially severe when one input row fans out to many outputs. ### Why `flat_map` is not sufficient `flat_map` expresses the logical row expansion, but it does not make each returned row a physical block. Ray Data can accumulate the returned rows into one or more larger output blocks. Yielding rows changes when rows are produced, but does not establish a one-row physical block boundary either. A downstream `map_batches(..., batch_size=1)` does not repair this: `batch_size` controls the batches passed to the UDF inside a map worker, not the number of independently schedulable Ray tasks or actor calls. The only general Ray Data sequence we have found that establishes the required physical scheduling boundaries is therefore: ```python dataset = ( source .map_batches(fanout) .repartition(target_num_rows_per_block=1, strict=True) .map_batches(downstream, batch_size=1) ) ``` That sequence is unexpectedly slow at 10,000–100,000 output Tasks and can leave downstream CPU and GPU workers underutilized. ### Standalone reproduction This does not import any application framework. It uses the default `DataContext`, normal Ray compute strategies, and `TaskPoolStrategy(size=1)` for the initial 1 -> M partitioning-shaped stage. ```python import time from dataclasses import dataclass import ray from ray.data import TaskPoolStrategy @dataclass class Task: files: list[str] metadata: dict def fanout(batch: dict, outputs_per_input: int) -> dict: results = [] for parent in batch["item"]: for index in range(outputs_per_input): results.append( Task( files=[f"file-{index}"], metadata={"index": index}, ) ) return {"item": results} def downstream(batch: dict) -> dict: assert len(batch["item"]) == 1 return batch def run_shape(num_input_blocks: int, outputs_per_input: int) -> None: rows = [ { "item": Task( files=[f"seed-{index}"], metadata={"parent_index": index}, ) } for index in range(num_input_blocks) ] source = ray.data.from_items( rows, override_num_blocks=num_input_blocks, ) fanout_options = {} if num_input_blocks == 1: fanout_options["compute"] = TaskPoolStrategy(size=1) dataset = ( source .map_batches( fanout, fn_kwargs={"outputs_per_input": outputs_per_input}, **fanout_options, ) .repartition(target_num_rows_per_block=1, strict=True) .map_batches(downstream, batch_size=1) ) start = time.perf_counter() result = dataset.materialize() elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start expected = num_input_blocks * outputs_per_input # Private API used only to verify the physical-block contract in this repro. block_rows = result._block_num_rows() assert len(block_rows) == expected assert block_rows == [1] * expected print( f"{num_input_blocks} x {outputs_per_input}: " f"{expected} one-row blocks in {elapsed:.2f}s" ) ray.init() # Initial fanout: one partitioning-shaped task produces all downstream Tasks. run_shape(num_input_blocks=1, outputs_per_input=10_000) # Middle fanout: existing one-row Task blocks each expand into more Tasks. run_shape(num_input_blocks=100, outputs_per_input=100) ``` Increasing either shape to 100,000 outputs is useful for making the throughput problem obvious: ```python run_shape(num_input_blocks=1, outputs_per_input=100_000) run_shape(num_input_blocks=100, outputs_per_input=1_000) ``` On a 32-CPU machine using Ray master at `9c6ffee9a5126a21dc529eceb02e2fa3e8b9183e`, representative master runs took: - 1 x 100,000: 624.50 seconds - 100 x 1,000: 223.51 seconds Both produced exactly 100,000 physical blocks with exactly one row per block. These are representative single master measurements; repeated measurements are included below for the experimental paths. The problem also affects useful downstream work. With four autoscaling actor workers doing 20 ms of work per item, avoidable delivery/control overhead left substantial actor capacity idle. ### Expected behavior Creating 100,000 independently scheduled work units necessarily has O(number of work units) scheduling, metadata, serialization, and object-store cost. We are not expecting this to be free or asking Ray Data to hide multiple Tasks inside larger blocks. We expect: - exactly one output row in every physical block; - each output to remain independently schedulable; - fanout delivery to provide enough runway to keep downstream task and actor pools busy; - no requirement for users to choose an internal chunk/window size; and - materially lower end-to-end overhead for both 1 -> M and N -> N*M fanout. ### AI-assisted deep dive The following is an AI-assisted investigation and working diagnosis, separate from the user-facing reproduction above. There appear to be two distinct per-output control costs: 1. **Low-producer repartition delivery.** A `StreamingRepartition` task returns every one-row block and its metadata through a streaming generator. The default two-object generator window corresponds to only one logical output block plus its metadata. In a 1 -> 100,000 fanout, one producer repeatedly performs the worker/Core/executor capacity handshake for every output. 2. **Downstream one-output map delivery.** Each downstream task or actor call also uses a streaming generator, even in the narrow case where the plan knows it consumes one row and the UDF declares that it preserves row count. Such a call can only return one block, but still pays generator polling and end-of-stream handling per work item. A fork-only experimental draft tested two correspondingly narrow changes: an input-size-derived, capped repartition generator runway, and ordinary fixed Ray returns for maps proven to produce exactly one block. It did not change the one-row physical-block contract or increase the global actor queue depth. Observed results: | Shape / downstream | Existing behavior | Experimental path | Improvement | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 x 100,000, no-op tasks | 624.50s | 205.86s median | 3.03x | | 100 x 1,000, no-op tasks | 223.51s | 185.10s median | 1.21x | | 100 x 100, four actors at 20ms/item | 139.80s median | 91.95s median | 1.52x | For the actor-shaped 10,000-item comparison, mean useful actor utilization increased from about 36.7% to 56.0%, while all four actors processed approximately equal numbers of items. Experimental code and benchmark details: https://github.com/praateekmahajan/ray/pull/1 Negative results from the same investigation: - Incremental `flat_map` improved first-output latency but made repeated total end-to-end time worse. - Naively fusing fanout and repartition also made total time worse. - Increasing actor tasks-in-flight helped this workload but has global memory and backpressure costs, so it is not a general fix. - Grouping block and metadata generator returns reduced report RPCs in isolation but regressed full-pipeline time. ### Distinction from related reports - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65433 tracks fair-share allocation overstating currently runnable task-pool demand. That can interact with downstream utilization, but it is a separate resource-allocation problem and does not explain the repeated per-output delivery cost. - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65434 and https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65436 track rebuilding the local `BlockOutputBuffer` remainder for every row-sized output. Avoiding those rebuilds improves the slicing microbenchmark, but changed a 1,000-item end-to-end pipeline only from a 18.34s median to 18.05s in that PR. It does not materially address the full fanout pipeline. - The downstream-capacity-ratio behavior is also independent, although it may amplify underutilization. ### Versions / Dependencies Reproduced on Ray master at `9c6ffee9a5126a21dc529eceb02e2fa3e8b9183e`. The original application workload was also observed on Ray 2.55–2.56-era builds. ### Issue Severity High for pipelines that use rows as independently scheduled CPU/GPU work units: the pipeline makes progress and is correct, but fanout delivery can take minutes and leave expensive downstream resources underutilized.

signal.title: [serve][llm] s3:// model_source is dropped on Ray 2.57.0: engine config gets model_id instead of the staged local path
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen An `LLMConfig` with an `s3://` `model_source` and `load_format="runai_streamer"` fails to deploy on Ray 2.57.0. `_get_vllm_engine_config` receives the **`model_id` alias** (`qwen-0.5b`) instead of the staged local path, so vLLM resolves the alias as a Hugging Face repo id and errors. The weights are never staged: on 2.56.0 the engine logs `model='/home/ray/.cache/vllm/assets/model_streamer/<hash>'`; on 2.57.0 that directory is empty on every node. Same script and cluster shape work on 2.56.0. Possibly a regression of #51617 (engine config recreated instead of reusing the one with `hf_model_id` set to the downloaded path). ### Versions / Dependencies Ray 2.57.0 (`anyscale/ray-llm:2.57.0-py312-cu130`), vLLM 0.25.1, torch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, `runai-model-streamer` / `runai-model-streamer-s3` 0.16.1. Works on Ray 2.56.0 / vLLM 0.22.0. ### Reproduction script ```python from ray import serve from ray.serve.llm import LLMConfig, build_openai_app llm_config = LLMConfig( model_loading_config=dict( model_id="qwen-0.5b", model_source="s3://anyscale-public-materials-use2/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", ), deployment_config=dict(autoscaling_config=dict(min_replicas=1, max_replicas=1)), runtime_env=dict(env_vars={"AWS_REGION": "us-east-2"}), engine_kwargs=dict(load_format="runai_streamer", max_model_len=4096, enforce_eager=True), ) serve.run(build_openai_app({"llm_configs": [llm_config]})) ``` Traceback, Serve LLM frames only: ``` File "ray/llm/_internal/serve/core/server/llm_server.py", line 277, in _start_engine await self.engine.start() File "ray/llm/_internal/serve/engines/vllm/vllm_engine.py", line 365, in start ) = self._prepare_engine_config(callback.ctx) File "ray/llm/_internal/serve/engines/vllm/vllm_engine.py", line 538, in _prepare_engine_config vllm_engine_args, vllm_engine_config = ray.get(ref) ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(RuntimeError): ray::_get_vllm_engine_config() File "ray/llm/_internal/serve/engines/vllm/vllm_engine.py", line 198, in _get_vllm_engine_config raise RuntimeError(f"Failed to create vLLM engine config: {e}") from None RuntimeError: Failed to create vLLM engine config: qwen-0.5b is not a local folder and is not a valid model identifier listed on 'https://huggingface.co/models' ``` ### Notes - Intermittent: ~1 success in 8 deploys of the identical config. Not a cold-cache effect, it also fails with weights already staged by an earlier success. - A plain HF `model_source` deploys reliably, isolating this to the S3 staging path. - Not disk (120+ GB free per node) and not a missing streamer package. - `raise ... from None` at `vllm_engine.py:198` drops the underlying exception, so the message names the alias rather than the staging failure that caused it. ### Issue Severity High: blocks serving models from S3.
signal.author: Aydin-ab

signal.title: [docs] Convert the nine highest-traffic landing pages from RST to MyST
signal.text:
## Why are these changes needed? MyST Markdown is the standard for Ray doc pages, and a lint check already rejects newly-added `.rst`. This is the first batch of the conversion of the existing hand-written prose under `doc/source/`. The batch is the nine highest-traffic, lowest-risk pages in the tree: short prose intros plus a `toctree`, no tabs, no doctests, no includes. 679 lines total, and 23% of all `.rst` page views over the last 90 days. Starting here validates the conversion end to end on the pages where any regression is immediately obvious, at close to zero conversion risk. | File | Lines | | --- | --- | | `index.rst` | 27 | | `ray-overview/examples.rst` | 10 | | `ray-overview/use-cases.rst` | 187 | | `data/api/api.rst` | 22 | | `train/api/api.rst` | 256 | | `ray-core/key-concepts.rst` | 50 | | `cluster/key-concepts.rst` | 90 | | `ray-core/api/index.rst` | 15 | | `ray-overview/examples/index.rst` | 22 | The conversion is format-only. Every label name, `toctree` entry, directive, and prose line is preserved, so the rendered HTML should be unchanged and the preview-versus-`/en/master` diff should be empty. No URLs change: Sphinx maps `foo.rst` and `foo.md` to the same `foo.html`. ### Conversions worth a second look - **`index.rst` has no heading**, so its browser title comes entirely from `.. title:: Welcome to Ray!`. There's no MyST frontmatter equivalent, so it stays as RST in an `{eval-rst}` block. The file-level `:html_theme.sidebar_secondary.remove:` field becomes frontmatter, matching `404.md`. - **`train/api/api.rst` keeps its 19 `autosummary` directives and its `.. currentmodule::` as column-0 RST inside `{eval-rst}` blocks** — the pattern `serve/api/index.md` already uses. The two labels that sit directly above an `autosummary` stay inside the block so their targets still register. - **`ray-core/key-concepts.rst` has a two-item list that docutils folds into the preceding paragraph**, because no blank line separates them. [The rendered page](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/ray-core/key-concepts.html#environment-dependencies) shows it as one `

`. CommonMark *would* turn it into a real `

    `, so the leading `1.` and `2.` are escaped to keep the current rendering. Happy to unescape and let it become a real list if that's preferred, but that's a rendering change rather than a conversion. - **`use-cases.rst` keeps the `.. raw:: html` body of its two `query-param-ref` blocks as RST.** That directive parses its own content with a `docutils` parser at `doctree-resolved` time, independent of the host file's format, so the content has to stay RST either way. ## The CI change in the second commit Converting `data/api/api.rst` and `ray-core/api/index.rst` surfaced a real gap in `ci/ray_ci/doc/autodoc.py`, which is why this PR isn't docs-only. The API-discrepancy check builds each team's documented-API set by walking its landing page's `toctree`. The walker only recognized the RST directive form (`.. toctree::` followed by indented entries). A MyST `toctree` is a directive fence with entries at column 0, so the walker's "first unindented line ends the block" heuristic stops on the very first entry. The `data` and `core` teams would have walked no children at all, collapsing their documented set to the landing page itself and flagging every child page's `autosummary` entries as undocumented public APIs. `serve/api/index.md` was already Markdown, but it declares its whole surface inline with no page-level `toctree`, so this path had never been exercised. The second commit teaches the walker the fence form alongside the RST form, points the `data`, `core`, and `train` `head_doc_file` entries at the converted pages, and adds a regression test. The `toctree` entries themselves are unchanged, so the walk reaches exactly the same set of child files as before. The `.buildkite` rules fixtures and the two notebook links that named a converted file by path are refreshed in the same commit. The rules themselves match on directory prefix and on both extensions, so what each path emits is unchanged. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "MyST"` and a search for the converted paths return no other open PR touching these files or this conversion. #65469 is the companion skill change and is deliberately separate, so a rule change isn't buried in a content PR. AI assistance was used to prepare this change. ## Related issue number Part of the ongoing RST-to-MyST conversion of `doc/source/`. Subsequent batches follow the same traffic-weighted ordering. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] I've included any doc changes needed for the change. - [x] Testing strategy - [x] Unit tests: `ci/ray_ci/doc/test_autodoc.py` gains coverage for the MyST fence form; the walk over the three converted API landing pages was verified to reach the same child set as before. - [x] Release tests: not applicable. - [x] This PR is not tested (please justify below): the decisive check for the conversion itself is the Read the Docs preview build under `fail_on_warning: true`, plus a rendered diff against `/en/master`. Please hold the merge until both are confirmed clean.
signal.author: dstrodtman

signal.title: [doc] rst-to-myst: add a render-diff check and fix three mapping errors
signal.text:
## Why are these changes needed? The `rst-to-myst` skill treated a green `fail_on_warning` build as near-sufficient evidence that a conversion was faithful. It isn't, and #65467 proved it: converting the first batch of landing pages produced three regressions that built clean and emitted no warning anywhere. - **`doc/source/index.rst` carries its browser title in a `.. title::` directive.** That directive does not set the document title from inside an `{eval-rst}` block, so the site root rendered as ``. - **An RST `.. image::` with no `:alt:`** takes its alt text from the URI and emits a bare ``. The skill mapped it to `![](URL)`, which emits `alt=""` wrapped in a `

`. - **`default_role = "code"`** makes a single-backtick RST literal render as ``. The skill called the Markdown single-backtick "byte-faithful"; it drops the `code` class. None of the three is visible to a static source check, and none of them fails a build. The campaign has 345 files left to convert, so the fix has to be a check rather than a caution. ## What changed **`render_diff.py`** — fetches the RtD PR preview and `/en/master` for each page, extracts `

`, normalizes the host, release string, and search-highlight params, and diffs. ```bash python3 doc/.claude/skills/rst-to-myst/render_diff.py \ https://anyscale-ray--65467.com.readthedocs.build/en/65467/ \ index.html cluster/key-concepts.html ray-overview/use-cases.html ``` It filters the two differences every MyST page shows against an RST page, both verified inert: - `class="tex2jax_ignore mathjax_ignore"`, which myst-parser stamps on the root `
` of every MyST document. - The missing `code` class above. Grepping `pydata-sphinx-theme.css`, `theme.css`, and `doc/source/_static/css/` finds no rule for it, and every already-converted page in the tree renders without it. Plain backticks are the house choice; `--keep-benign` shows the difference if you want it. It also labels `ray-overview/examples.html`, which differs between *any* two builds because `custom_directives.py` picks its gallery icons with `random.randint`. **`SKILL.md`** — promotes the render diff from a one-line afterthought at the end of Verification to a required step, and says what it is for: steps 1–3 are all source-side or resolution-side, so step 4 is the only one that can catch this class. Corrects the `.. image::` mapping row, adds rows for `.. figure::` and `.. title::`, adds Hard rule 5 covering all three page-identity constructs, and rewrites the `default_role` construct note. The guidance is deliberately "read the diffs," not "expect zero." Byte-identical is not always the right bar — a caption-less `{figure}` or a deliberate alt-text addition shows up here too — so the question the script answers is whether every diff is explainable. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "rst-to-myst"` returns no open PR touching this skill or `doc/.claude/skills/`. #65467 is the content batch that motivated this; it deliberately does not carry the skill change, since a rule change buried in a content PR ships unreviewed. ## Related issue number Follow-up to #65467. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] I've included any doc changes needed for the change. - [x] Testing strategy - **Commands run and results.** `python3 render_diff.py --help` parses. Run against #65467's preview across all nine converted pages, it reports `index.html`, `cluster/key-concepts.html`, and `ray-overview/use-cases.html` as `IDENTICAL` after the fixes and correctly flags `ray-overview/examples.html` as known-nondeterministic. Run against the same preview *before* those fixes, it surfaced all three regressions above, which is how they were found. Benign-class filtering verified in both directions with and without `--keep-benign`. - Release tests: not applicable. - This PR touches `doc/.claude/` only, which no Bazel target or `.buildkite` rule references, so it pulls no CI suite. AI assistance was used to prepare this change.

signal.title: [docs] Convert the seven card-grid library front doors from RST to MyST
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? MyST Markdown is the standard for Ray doc pages, and a lint check already rejects newly-added `.rst`. This is the second batch of the conversion of the existing hand-written prose under `doc/source/`, following #65467. The batch is the seven library front-door pages. They share one pattern: a `grid` of `grid-item-card`s, some `tab-set`s, `literalinclude` pulls, and a `toctree`. 1,889 lines, and 18% of all `.rst` page views over the last 90 days. | File | Lines | Constructs | | --- | --- | --- | | `tune/index.rst` | 299 | 3 tabs, 6 cards, 3 literalinclude, `callout`/`annotations` | | `ray-core/walkthrough.rst` | 132 | 3 cards, 4 literalinclude | | `data/data.rst` | 187 | 5 cards, 1 testcode | | `train/train.rst` | 233 | 10 cards, nested `div`, `raw:: html :file:` | | `ray-overview/installation.rst` | 548 | 2 tab-sets, 3 tables, 20 named link targets | | `ray-overview/ray-libraries.rst` | 378 | 17 cards | | `cluster/getting-started.rst` | 112 | 4 cards | The conversion is format-only. Every label name, `toctree` entry, directive, and prose line is preserved, so the rendered HTML should be unchanged. No URLs change: Sphinx maps `foo.rst` and `foo.md` to the same `foo.html`. Unlike #65467, this batch needs no CI or `BUILD.bazel` changes. None of the seven files is named in `doc/BUILD.bazel`, in a `.buildkite` rules fixture, or in `ci/ray_ci/doc`. `data/data.rst`'s one real `testcode`/`testoutput` pair stays covered by the `data` doctest rule's `source/**/*.md` glob. ## Card grids convert to native MyST Every card grid already in a `.md` page (`cluster/vms/index.md`, `cluster/kubernetes/index.md`, `ray-overview/index.md`, `serve/index.md`) is wrapped in `{eval-rst}` and left as RST. This batch uses native MyST fences instead: ```markdown ::::{grid} 1 2 2 2 :gutter: 1 :::{grid-item-card} **Title** ^^^ Body text. +++ ```{button-ref} some-label :color: primary Button text ``` ::: :::: ``` sphinx-design supports MyST first-class — its own docs are MyST and it ships a `snippets/myst/` tree. The `^^^` and `+++` separators are matched by `REGEX_HEADER`/`REGEX_FOOTER` and split out of the raw content lines before anything parses them, so they're format-agnostic. `GridDirective` and `GridItemCardDirective` are ordinary docutils directives registered through `app.add_directive`, which MyST dispatches exactly the way it already dispatches `{tab-set}` in a dozen `.md` pages today. The one thing to know: these directives call `self.state.nested_parse`, so under MyST their content parses as **Markdown**. Any RST left inside a native card renders as literal text instead of erroring. That's why the nested `button-ref`/`button-link`/`image`/`figure` directives all convert too, and it's the specific thing the render diff below was run to confirm. A follow-up PR converts the four existing `{eval-rst}`-wrapped grids so the tree ends up with one pattern rather than two. ## Conversions worth a second look - **`installation.rst` keeps its RST simple table in `{eval-rst}`.** The nightly-wheel table for Linux is a `====`-delimited simple table whose cells are RST named-target references. Converting it to a Markdown or `{list-table}` table changes the rendered HTML, so it stays RST along with the eight target definitions it uses, which now live in the same block. The MacOS and Windows tabs were already `list-table`s, so those become `{list-table}` with the URLs inlined as Markdown links. - **`tune/index.rst` had two link forms that don't survive transcription.** `` `Ray Serve`_ `` pointed at `../serve/index.html`, a relative `.html` URL that renders in RST but is a cross-reference target under MyST; it becomes `` {doc}`Ray Serve </serve/index>` ``. Separately, `` `terminating bad runs early <tune-scheduler-hyperband>`_ `` is an RST *external* link to a bare label name, so today it renders as `<a href="tune-scheduler-hyperband">` — a dead relative URL. Sibling lines in the same paragraph use `:ref:` for the same targets, so it becomes `{ref}`. **That is a deliberate rendering change and the one place the diff below is not empty.** Happy to keep the dead link if you'd rather this PR stay strictly format-only. - **`tune/index.rst` is the only file in the tree using the `callout` and `annotations` directives** (`doc/source/_ext/callouts.py`). Both `nested_parse`, so their content is now Markdown; the `<1>`/`<2>` annotation markers are literal text under both parsers. - **`train/train.rst`'s logo block** nests `div` inside `div` around a `raw:: html` with a `:file:` option. It converts to nested colon fences with a `{raw}` fence inside. - **`ray-overview/getting-started.md` linked to `../tune/index.rst`**, which would dangle after the rename. It becomes a `{doc}` reference. ## Verification - Static checks pass on all seven files: frontmatter parses, backtick and colon fences balance at every width, all 14 labels preserved, no residual RST outside fences, no `.rst`/`.html#` link forms, `testcode`/`testoutput` counts match the originals. - Read the Docs preview under `fail_on_warning: true`. - `render_diff.py` against `/en/master` for all seven pages. **Please hold the merge until I've posted those results in a comment.** ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open` shows no other PR touching these seven files or this conversion, other than #65468, which changes six lines inside `installation.rst`'s extras table. Whichever lands first, the other rebases. ## Related issue number Part of the ongoing RST-to-MyST conversion of `doc/source/`, following #65467. Subsequent batches follow the same traffic-weighted ordering. AI assistance was used to prepare this change. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] I've included any doc changes needed for the change. - [x] Testing strategy - [x] Unit tests: not applicable; no `BUILD.bazel` or CI wiring changes in this batch. - [x] Release tests: not applicable. - [x] This PR is not tested (please justify below): the decisive checks for a conversion are the RtD preview build under `fail_on_warning: true` and the rendered diff against `/en/master`, both listed above.

signal.title: [doc] rst-to-myst: add the sphinx-design card-grid mapping
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Stacked on #65469. Converting the seven card-grid front doors in #65470 exercised a part of the `rst-to-myst` skill that had no mapping at all: `grid`, `grid-item-card`, `grid-item`, `button-ref`, `button-link`, and `div`. The skill covered sphinx-design tabs and dropdowns but stopped short of cards, which are the dominant construct in batches 4 through 8. It also had no entry for RST named hyperlink targets (`` `text`_ `` plus a `.. _`text`: url` definition). `ray-overview/installation.rst` alone has twenty. ## What changed **Mapping rows** for the six sphinx-design directives above. **A construct note on card grids**, covering the two things that aren't obvious: - The `^^^` header and `+++` footer separators need no translation. sphinx-design matches them with `REGEX_HEADER`/`REGEX_FOOTER` in `cards.py` and splits them out of the raw content lines before anything parses them, so they're format-agnostic. - `GridDirective`, `GridItemCardDirective`, `div`, and Ray's own `callout`/`annotations` all call `self.state.nested_parse`, which under MyST parses their content as **Markdown**. RST left inside a native card doesn't warn — it renders as literal text through a green `fail_on_warning` build. Everything nested has to convert in the same pass, and the render diff is the only check that catches it. That second point also fixes a dangling reference: Verification step 4 already said the render diff is "the only step that catches Hard rule 5 or the `nested_parse` degradation below," and there was no such note below. Now there is. The note also records that four already-Markdown pages (`cluster/vms/index.md`, `cluster/kubernetes/index.md`, `ray-overview/index.md`, `serve/index.md`) wrap their grids in `{eval-rst}`, and says not to copy that into new conversions. A follow-up PR converts those four. **A construct note on named hyperlink targets** — inline them as Markdown links, except where an `{eval-rst}` table's cells reference them, in which case the definitions stay RST inside that same block so no target name is defined twice. **Two verified facts**, both checked against the pinned source rather than assumed: - `sphinx_design==0.7.0` supports MyST first-class. Its own docs are MyST, it ships a `snippets/myst/` tree, and its directives register through `app.add_directive`, so MyST's `{name}` dispatch reaches them like any other directive. - `_replace_numbers()` in `doc/source/_ext/callouts.py` discards its own result (`content.replace(...)` with no assignment), so the `<1>`-to-① substitution only happens in `CalloutIncludePostTransform`, over literal blocks. Annotation text keeps literal `<1>` markers under either parser. Flagging rather than fixing, since it's outside this PR's scope and the rendering is longstanding. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "rst-to-myst"` returns #65469, which this is stacked on and which touches different sections of the same file. No other open PR touches `doc/.claude/skills/`. ## Related issue number Follow-up to #65469. Motivated by #65470, which deliberately doesn't carry this change, since a rule change buried in a content PR ships unreviewed. AI assistance was used to prepare this change. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] I've included any doc changes needed for the change. - [x] Testing strategy - The claims about `^^^`/`+++` splitting, `nested_parse`, and directive registration were read off `sphinx_design==0.7.0`'s own source (`cards.py`, `grids.py`, `extension.py`), not inferred. The native-grid pattern the note prescribes is the one #65470 ships and render-diffs. - Release tests: not applicable. - This PR touches `doc/.claude/` only, which no Bazel target or `.buildkite` rule references, so it pulls no CI suite.

signal.title: [doc] Convert the four remaining wrapped card grids to native MyST
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Stacked on #65470. Four pages are already Markdown but keep their sphinx-design card grids as RST inside an `{eval-rst}` block: | File | Cards | | --- | --- | | `cluster/kubernetes/index.md` | 6 | | `serve/index.md` | 5 | | `cluster/vms/index.md` | 4 | | `ray-overview/index.md` | 3 | That pattern predates native MyST card support and, until #65470, was the only card-grid precedent in the tree. Now that the seven highest-traffic front doors use native fences, these four are the remainder. Converting them leaves one pattern instead of two, so batches 4 through 8 have an unambiguous model to copy. ## What changed Each `{eval-rst}` grid becomes native colon fences, widest on the outside: ```markdown ::::{grid} 1 2 2 2 :gutter: 1 :class-container: container pb-3 :::{grid-item-card} :class-img-top: pt-2 w-75 d-block mx-auto fixed-height-img **Getting Started** ^^^ Body text. +++ ```{button-ref} some-label :color: primary :outline: :expand: Button text ``` ::: :::: ``` Format-only. Grid and card options, the `^^^` and `+++` separators, and every `button-ref` target are preserved verbatim. **The one non-mechanical part:** a native card's content parses as Markdown, not RST, so the `:doc:` and `:ref:` roles in the card bodies had to become `{doc}` and `{ref}` in the same pass. Left as RST they wouldn't warn — they'd render as literal text through a green build. `ray-overview/index.md` has six `:doc:` roles in one card and `serve/index.md` has ten `:ref:` roles across five, so this is the bulk of the non-whitespace diff. The separate `{eval-rst}` block in `cluster/kubernetes/index.md` holding an `.. image::` and a source-document comment is left alone. It isn't a grid, and folding it in would widen this PR past its stated scope. ## Verification - Fence balance checked at every colon width on all four files; backtick fences even; no residual `:doc:`/`:ref:`/``` `` ``` RST outside fences. - Read the Docs preview under `fail_on_warning: true`. - `render_diff.py` against `/en/master` for all four pages. **Please hold the merge until I've posted those results in a comment** — the render diff is the only check that catches a card whose nested content silently degraded. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open` shows no other PR touching these four files. ## Related issue number Follows #65470. The mapping and the `nested_parse` caveat behind this change are documented in #65471. AI assistance was used to prepare this change. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (`git commit -s`). - [x] I've run `scripts/format.sh` to lint the changes in this PR. - [x] I've included any doc changes needed for the change. - [x] Testing strategy - [x] Unit tests: not applicable; no CI or `BUILD.bazel` wiring changes. - [x] Release tests: not applicable. - [x] This PR is not tested (please justify below): the decisive checks for a format conversion are the RtD preview under `fail_on_warning: true` and the rendered diff against `/en/master`, both listed above.

signal.title: [Core] Fix prepared bundle leak and scheduling stall when removing an in-flight placement group
signal.text: ## Description Removing a placement group while bundle preparation is still in flight can leak prepared raylet resources and leave the GCS placement-group scheduling gate stuck. The scheduler already documents that a `PrepareBundleResources` callback may never fire (e.g. when the target node dies), but cancellation and removal still waited on that callback: - `MarkScheduleCancelled` only recorded the cancelled state; already-prepared bundles were not released because cleanup waited for `OnAllBundlePrepareRequestReturned`, which requires *all* prepare callbacks to return. - A prepare reply arriving after cancellation was folded into the tracker but still waited for the remaining callbacks before any cleanup ran. - `RemovePlacementGroup` never released `scheduling_in_progress_id_`, so a later pending placement group was never scheduled. This change makes cancellation- and removal-time cleanup independent of the prepare callbacks that may never arrive: - `MarkScheduleCancelled` now destroys the already-prepared bundles immediately (skipped only while committing, where the commit path already handles cleanup). - A prepare reply that returns after cancellation releases the just-prepared bundle immediately instead of waiting for the remaining callbacks. - `RemovePlacementGroup` releases the scheduling token it owns, and the creation callbacks only release the token when the callback's placement group still owns it, so a stale callback from a removed group cannot clear a newer group's token. ## Related issues Fixes #64693 ## Additional information No API or wire-format changes. The regression tests model a prepare callback that never returns by withholding the reply on the mock raylet client, so they are deterministic. ## Tests - `bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_scheduler_test --test_filter=GcsPlacementGroupSchedulerTest.PlacementGroupCancelledAfterPartialPrepareReleasesPreparedBundle --test_output=errors` — fails on master (no `RemovePlacementGroupBundles` RPC for the already-prepared bundle), passes with this change. - `bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_scheduler_test --test_filter=GcsPlacementGroupSchedulerTest.PlacementGroupCancelledAfterLatePrepareSuccessReleasesNewBundle --test_output=errors` — fails on master, passes with this change. - `bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test --test_filter=GcsPlacementGroupManagerTest.TestRemovingLeasingPlacementGroupUnblocksPending --test_output=errors` — fails on master (the pending placement group is never scheduled), passes with this change. - `bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test --test_filter=GcsPlacementGroupManagerTest.TestLateCallbackDoesNotReleaseNextPlacementGroupToken --test_output=errors` — covers the scheduling-token guard: a late creation callback from a removed placement group must not release the token a newer group now owns. Fails on master, passes with this change. - The surrounding placement-group cancellation tests in both files (`DestroyCancelledPlacementGroup`, `PlacementGroupCancelledDuringCommit`, `PlacementGroupCancelledDuringPreparedPut`, `TestRemovingLeasingPlacementGroup`) pass.

signal.title: [Data] Add DataIterator.count() to get dataset/shard size
signal.text: ## Description Add a public `DataIterator.count()` that returns the number of rows the iterator will yield, so users (notably Ray Train workers that receive a shard via `ray.train.get_dataset_shard()`) can size LR schedulers, progress bars, or max training steps without consuming the iterator. Previously the only options were exhausting the iterator or calling `it._base_dataset.count()`. - `DataIteratorImpl` (from `Dataset.iterator()`) delegates to `Dataset.count()`, reading Parquet file metadata where possible (no data scan). - `StreamSplitDataIterator` (from `Dataset.streaming_split()`) returns the per-shard count for `equal=True` splits (`total_rows // num_splits`, exact since the output splitter drops the remainder). For `equal=False` the per-split count is only known at runtime, so it raises `NotImplementedError` pointing users to `count()` on the source `Dataset`. It also raises if called while the split is being actively iterated. - The base `DataIterator.count()` is a `@PublicAPI` method that raises `NotImplementedError` by default, so existing third-party subclasses are unaffected. ## Related issues Closes #37634 ## Test plan - [x] `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_iterator.py::test_iterator_count -v` - [x] `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_iterator.py::test_iterator_count_after_transform -v` - [x] `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_streaming_integration.py::test_streaming_split_count_equal -v` - [x] `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_streaming_integration.py::test_streaming_split_count_not_equal_raises -v` - [x] `pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_streaming_integration.py::test_streaming_split_count_during_execution_raises -v`

signal.title: [Fix/n] Return External Consumer Bytes for Downstream Capacity to Activate Backpressure
signal.text: ## Description #64456 applies the block ref counter to track the object store memory and control backpressure signals based on downstream capacity, but this had lead to spilling in training pipelines. This is mainly due to backpressure not being applied to the terminal operator even though the external consumer is not consuming blocks quickly enough. This PR adds back the early return for `DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy`'s `_get_downstream_capacity_size_bytes`, so that for terminal operators, the downstream capacity is the external consumer bytes tracked instead of 0. ## Related issues Fixes https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/64456.
